text: Here is an array of five numbers: five, two, nine, one, and seven. They are in no particular order, and our goal is to rearrange them so they climb steadily from smallest to largest. There are many ways to do this. The one we are going to build today is arguably the simplest thing that could possibly work.

The entire algorithm rests on a single rule. Look at two neighboring numbers. If the left one is bigger than the right one, swap them. That is it. No global view of the array, no clever bookkeeping. Just one local comparison, repeated patiently.

So we start at the left edge, and compare five and two. Five is bigger than two, so by our rule these two are in the wrong order, and we swap them. Notice that the array is not sorted yet. But it is, in one small way, more sorted than it was a moment ago.

Now slide one step to the right and repeat. Five against nine: five is smaller, so this pair is already fine, and we leave it alone. Slide again. Nine against one, clearly out of order, so we swap. And watch what is happening to that nine. It keeps winning its comparisons, so it keeps moving to the right.

One more comparison: nine against seven. Nine wins again, and slides into the final position. This is the key insight of the pass. The largest number, wherever it happened to start, gets carried all the way to the end. It bubbles up. And that is where the name comes from.

Which means we now know something permanent. Nine is in its final resting place. Nothing in the rest of the array could possibly be larger, so we never need to look at it again. We mark it as settled, and shrink our working region by one.

Now we simply do the whole thing again on what is left. Two against five: fine. Five against one: swap. Five against seven: fine. And once again the largest of the remaining numbers, seven, has been carried to the end of the region. Two numbers are now locked in place.

The pattern should be clear now, and notice that each pass is cheaper than the one before it. Two against one: swap. Two against five: fine. Five settles into position, and our unsorted region has shrunk to just the first two entries.
One final comparison. One against two, already in order. And with that, there is nothing left that could possibly be out of place. The array is sorted: one, two, five, seven, nine.

Now step back and count the work. Each pass walks across the array once, and we need roughly one pass per element. That gives us about n passes of about n comparisons each, so the total cost grows like n squared. Double the size of the input, and you roughly quadruple the work.

And that is the trade. Bubble sort is far too slow for serious data, and real sorting algorithms do dramatically better. But it earns its place as a first algorithm, because it shows how a rule simple enough to fit in a single sentence, applied patiently enough times, can impose complete order on chaos.
